photos.question: The nurse is preparing to give IV potassium chloride to a client with hypokalemia. Which action is correct?
photos.caption:
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #252!

💉 Can IV potassium ever be pushed?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Dilute It and Infuse with a Pump

🧠 Rationale: IV potassium is never given by IV push.

A fast dose can cause deadly dysrhythmias and cardiac arrest.

It must be diluted and run slowly on an infusion pump.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: IV Potassium Chloride

💊 Drug Class: Electrolyte replacement

❤️ Primary Use: Treating low potassium (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L)

⚠️ Watch For:

🔹 Burning or pain at the IV site

🔹 Peaked T waves if the level goes too high

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Always use an infusion pump

✅ Check kidney function and urine output first

✅ Keep the client on a cardiac monitor for higher rates

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Potassium: never push, always pump!

❤️ Follow @ryan__glass for daily NCLEX practice questions!

photos.question: Which finding should the nurse expect in a client with Addison disease?
photos.caption:
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #253!

🧬 Low cortisol can change the color of the skin. Do you know how?

This is a HIGH-YIELD endocrine question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Bronze or Darkened Skin

🧠 Rationale: Addison disease is adrenal insufficiency: too little cortisol and aldosterone.

High ACTH levels darken the skin, giving a bronze look.

Moon face and weight gain point to Cushing syndrome instead.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Addison Disease

❤️ What Happens: The adrenal glands make too little cortisol and aldosterone

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Bronze skin

🔹 Weight loss and fatigue

🔹 Low sodium, high potassium, low glucose

🔹 Low blood pressure

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Teach lifelong steroid replacement

✅ Never stop steroids suddenly

✅ Extra doses may be needed during illness or stress

🚑 Emergency: Addisonian crisis causes severe low BP and shock. Expect IV fluids and IV hydrocortisone.

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Addison = Adding bronze to the skin, losing sodium and weight!

❤️ Follow @ryan__glass for daily NCLEX practice questions!

#NCLEX #NursingSchool #NCLEXPrep #Endocrine #AddisonDisease #Adrenal #MedSurg #NursingStudent #FutureRN #NursingEducation

photos.question: Before giving metoprolol, which finding should make the nurse hold the dose and contact the provider?
photos.caption:
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #254!

❤️ What vital sign do you ALWAYS check before a beta blocker?

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiac question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Heart Rate 52 Beats per Minute

🧠 Rationale: Metoprolol is a beta blocker that lowers heart rate and blood pressure.

A heart rate below 60 usually means hold the dose and call the provider.

The other vital signs are within normal limits.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Metoprolol

💊 Drug Class: Beta blocker (the "olol" drugs)

❤️ Primary Use: High blood pressure, angina, heart failure, after a heart attack

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Bradycardia

🔹 Low blood pressure and dizziness

🔹 Can hide signs of low blood sugar

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check apical pulse and BP before every dose

✅ Teach slow position changes

✅ Never stop the drug suddenly

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

"Olol" drugs slow the heart: check the pulse before you give it!

❤️ Follow @ryan__glass for daily NCLEX practice questions!

#NCLEX #NursingSchool #NCLEXPrep #Cardiac #BetaBlockers #Metoprolol #Pharmacology #NursingStudent #FutureRN #NursingEducation

photos.question: A client with a chest injury is becoming more short of breath. Which finding suggests a tension pneumothorax?
photos.caption:
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #255!

🫁 One finding in the neck can signal a lung emergency. Do you know it?

This is a HIGH-YIELD respiratory question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Trachea Shifted Away from the Injured Side

🧠 Rationale: In tension pneumothorax, trapped air builds pressure in the chest.

That pressure pushes the trachea and heart toward the unaffected side.

This lowers cardiac output and can quickly cause shock.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Tension Pneumothorax

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Tracheal deviation

🔹 Absent breath sounds on the injured side

🔹 Severe shortness of breath

🔹 Low BP and fast heart rate

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Call the rapid response team

✅ Give high flow oxygen

✅ Prepare for needle decompression and a chest tube

🚑 Emergency: This can cause cardiac arrest within minutes.

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Tension pushes the trachea away from the trouble!

❤️ Follow @ryan__glass for daily NCLEX practice questions!

photos.question: A client has severe upper abdominal pain that radiates to the back. Which lab result best supports acute pancreatitis?
photos.caption:
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #256!

🔥 Pain radiating to the back. Which lab confirms it?

This is a HIGH-YIELD GI question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Elevated Serum Lipase

🧠 Rationale: The inflamed pancreas leaks enzymes into the blood.

Lipase is the most specific lab for acute pancreatitis.

Amylase rises too, but returns to normal sooner.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Acute Pancreatitis

❤️ Common Causes: Gallstones and heavy alcohol use

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back

🔹 Nausea and vomiting

🔹 Pain worse after eating

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ NPO to rest the pancreas

✅ IV fluids and pain control

✅ Monitor glucose and calcium

🚑 Watch For: Low calcium, shock and breathing problems

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Lipase = Lights up the pancreas!

❤️ Follow @ryan__glass for daily NCLEX practice questions!

photos.question: By what age should a healthy infant triple the birth weight?
photos.caption:
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #257!

👶 How fast should a baby grow in the first year?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pediatrics question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — 12 Months

🧠 Rationale: Healthy infants double their birth weight by about 5 to 6 months.

They triple their birth weight by about 12 months.

Slow weight gain should be checked for feeding or health problems.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Infant Growth

📏 Weight:

🔹 Double by 5 to 6 months

🔹 Triple by 12 months

📏 Length: Increases about 50 percent by 12 months

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Plot weight on a growth chart at every visit

✅ Ask about feeding and wet diapers

✅ Report falling off the growth curve

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Double by 6, triple by 12!

photos.question: Fifteen minutes into a blood transfusion, the client has chills, fever and low back pain. What should the nurse do first?
photos.caption:
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #258!

🩸 Chills and back pain during a transfusion. What comes FIRST?

This is a HIGH-YIELD safety question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Stop the Transfusion

🧠 Rationale: Chills, fever and low back pain suggest an acute transfusion reaction.

Stopping the blood right away limits how much enters the body.

Then keep the line open with normal saline and notify the provider and blood bank.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Blood Transfusion Reactions

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Chills and fever

🔹 Low back pain

🔹 Hives or itching

🔹 Shortness of breath or low BP

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Stop the transfusion

✅ Change the tubing and run normal saline

✅ Stay with the client and monitor vitals

✅ Send the blood bag back to the blood bank

⏱️ Key Fact: Most reactions happen in the first 15 minutes, so stay with the client

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Reaction? STOP the blood before anything else!

❤️ Follow @ryan__glass for daily NCLEX practice questions!
